Persons or class of persons entitled to drive:

As per Section 2(47), "transport vehicle" means "a public service vehicle, a goods
carriage, an educational institution bus or a private service vehicle."
16. Although the definition of the 'light motor vehicle' brings within its umbrage both 'transport

args.question: We are National Insurance Co. The deceased's family claims compensation for a death caused by our insured's truck, whose driver had no valid driving licence. What precedents support our defence, and what authorities cut against us?

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving a motor vehicle without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy, absolving the insurer of direct liability to the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had no driving licence at all on the date of accident — identical to our case. The tribunal held the insurer proved the breach under Section 149(2) and was not directly liable.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the strongest supporting authority in the corpus. It squarely holds that a complete absence of a licence is a 'fundamental breach' and the insurer is not liable to indemnify the insured. The pay-and-recover direction was given only because the claimant was a third party.
supporting.quote: riding/driving vehicle on public road without having driving license it is not only an offense punishable under section 3(1) r/w 181 of MV Act but also fundamental and statutory breach of insurance policy. Hence, the respondent No.2 is not liable to pay the compensation and he is absolved from its liability.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar
supporting.principle: Where a driving licence had expired and was renewed more than 30 days after expiry, the renewal operates only from the date of renewal, not retrospectively, so the driver had no valid licence on the accident date.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver's licence had expired before the accident and was renewed only after a gap exceeding 30 days — analogous to 'no valid licence' on the accident date. The court held the insurer could pay and recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Establishes that an expired licence not renewed within the 30-day grace period means the driver had no effective licence. The insurer's defence of breach is valid, though pay-and-recover was ordered for third-party protection.
supporting.quote: as on the date of accident, the driver of offending Maruthi Omni was not having valid and effective driving license... the insurance company shall pay the amount and recover the same from driver or the insured.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where the driver held only an LMV licence without authorisation to drive a transport vehicle, there is a breach of policy conditions, but the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver lacked the proper licence category for the vehicle — analogous to our 'no valid licence' scenario. The court recognised the breach but applied pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Confirms that licence deficiency (even short of complete absence) is a recognised breach. The insurer's defence is valid; the only question is whether the court orders pay-and-recover.
supporting.quote: the 3rd Respondent had a licence, but not a valid one... there was violation of Policy conditions.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
supporting.principle: Absence of a mandatory special endorsement on a driving licence constitutes a breach of policy conditions entitling the insurer to pay and recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver lacked the required endorsement — a licence defect. The court reversed the tribunal's finding and granted pay-and-recover rights to the insurer.
supporting.why_it_matters: Shows that courts will recognise licence defects as breaches and grant recovery rights. Supports our argument that the absence of a valid licence is a real breach.
supporting.quote: once it was established that there was no such endorsement... it was a clear cut case of violation of terms and conditions of the insurance policy which entitled the insurance company to recover.

supporting.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
supporting.principle: The Swaran Singh principles apply only to third-party risks under Section 149. Where the licence was originally fake, renewal cannot cure the inherent fatality.
supporting.fact_alignment: While this case primarily concerns own-damage claims, it confirms that a fake licence cannot be cured by renewal — relevant if our driver's licence is found to be fake rather than merely absent.
supporting.why_it_matters: Provides an additional argument: if the licence was fake (not just absent), the insurer has an even stronger defence. Also confirms Swaran Singh's limits.
supporting.quote: Where originally the license was a fake one, renewal cannot cure the inherent fatality.

adverse.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
adverse.principle: The insurer has a statutory liability to satisfy a third-party award even if there is a breach of policy conditions (invalid driving licence), and is entitled to recover the amount from the insured.
adverse.risk_to_client: The opposing side will cite this to argue that even if the driver had no valid licence, National Insurance must pay the full award first, and can only recover from the owner afterwards. This defeats any argument that the insurer can walk away entirely.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This is the settled law from Swaran Singh and Kamla — we cannot avoid paying the third party. Our defence is limited to (a) proving the breach on record, and (b) securing a pay-and-recover order. We cannot argue for complete exoneration in a third-party death claim.
adverse.quote: the insurer has a statutory liability to pay the compensation to the third party and will simply have the right to recover the same from the insured/tortfeasor

adverse.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
adverse.principle: The insurer is statutorily liable to satisfy a third-party award regardless of policy condition breaches such as an expired driving licence; non-renewal of an otherwise valid licence is not a fundamental breach.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this to argue that an expired licence (or even no licence) does not absolve the insurer of third-party liability. The court held the insurer jointly and severally liable despite the driver having no effective licence on the accident date.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This judgment predates the clearer articulation of the pay-and-recover mechanism in later Supreme Court decisions. We can argue that the later line of authority (Satto, Sunil Killiket, Parvathi Hebbar) consistently recognises the breach and orders pay-and-recover rather than joint liability without recovery rights. However, the core point — that the insurer must pay the third party — remains good law.
adverse.quote: the insurance company is statutorily required to issue the policy... the liability to satisfy the award is statutory and not dependent upon the conditions imposed by the insurance company

adverse.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
adverse.principle: An insurer cannot avoid its statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties merely because the driver lacked a specific endorsement on their licence to drive a vehicle as a commercial vehicle.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this Supreme Court judgment to argue that licence deficiencies short of complete absence do not allow the insurer to escape liability. The court held the insurer liable even though the driver had no commercial vehicle endorsement.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: In Iyyapan, the driver did hold a valid LMV licence — the dispute was only about the missing commercial endorsement. In our case, the driver had no licence at all. The Supreme Court itself distinguished between 'no licence' and 'licence but missing endorsement'. The ratio is narrower than it appears.
adverse.quote: Merely because the driver did not get any endorsement in the driving licence to drive Mahindra Maxi Cab... the High Court has committed grave error of law in holding that the insurer is not liable

adverse.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
adverse.principle: In third-party claims, even if the driver lacks an appropriate endorsement to drive a specific heavy vehicle class, the insurer remains liable to satisfy the award and may recover from the insured.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this to argue that even if the driver had no valid licence for a heavy goods vehicle (truck), the insurer must still pay and can only recover from the owner. This directly applies to our truck scenario.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The driver in Chennamma held an LMV licence with a transport vehicle endorsement — the dispute was whether that covered a heavy goods vehicle. In our case, the driver had no licence at all, which is a more fundamental breach. The court in Chennamma itself noted that the driver did have some form of licence.
adverse.quote: the driver of the lorry had only licence to light motor vehicle... Tribunal held that Appellant-Insurance Company shall recover the same from the owner

adverse.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
adverse.principle: Even where the insurer proves a fundamental breach (no licence), the insurer must pay the third-party claimant first and then recover from the owner.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite the pay-and-recover direction in this very case to argue that National Insurance must pay the full compensation upfront. The case is double-edged: it supports our breach argument but compels payment.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: We do not dispute that we must pay the third party — our defence is that (a) the breach is established, (b) we are entitled to a pay-and-recover order, and (c) the owner bears ultimate liability. This case supports all three propositions.
adverse.quote: it is proper to direct the respondent No.2 to pay the compensation by reserving liberty to recover the same from the respondent No.1, owner of the offending vehicle

adverse.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar
adverse.principle: Even where the driver had no valid licence on the accident date, the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the insured.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this to show that even in a clear no-licence case, the insurer must pay first. This defeats any argument that the insurer can refuse payment entirely.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: Same as above — we accept the pay-and-recover framework. Our defence is about establishing the breach and securing recovery rights, not about avoiding payment to the claimant.
adverse.quote: the insurance company shall pay the amount and recover the same from driver or the insured

priority_arguments: 1. The driver had no valid driving licence at all — this is a fundamental and statutory breach of policy conditions under Section 149(2)(a)(ii) of the MV Act. Cite Sunil Shreesail Killiket (doc_024) which squarely holds that driving without a licence is a 'fundamental and statutory breach' and the insurer is 'absolved from its liability' to the insured.

2. Even if the court orders payment to the third party, we are entitled to a pay-and-recover order against the owner. Every single judgment in this corpus that involves a licence defect in a third-party claim grants recovery rights. There is no precedent in this corpus where the insurer was denied recovery rights after proving a licence breach.

3. The owner bears responsibility under Section 5 of the MV Act to ensure the driver holds a valid licence. The owner's failure to do so is the breach — not ours. The burden of proof is on us to show the breach, and we can discharge it through the charge sheet, RTO records, and the owner's failure to produce the licence.
4. If the licence turns out to be fake (rather than merely absent), cite Laxmi Narain Dhut (doc_031) for the proposition that a fake licence cannot be cured by subsequent renewal.
strategy.compensation_range: Cannot estimate without knowing the deceased's age, income, and number of dependents. The corpus shows awards ranging from approximately Rs. 12-13 lakhs (Chennamma, doc_027) to Rs. 99 lakhs (Sunil Killiket, doc_024 — though that was an injury case). Use compute_quantum tool with actual facts.
strategy.compensation_reasoning: Quantum will be computed under Sarla Verma / Pranay Sethi framework. Our defence does not challenge quantum — it challenges liability. However, we should verify the multiplier and dependency calculation to ensure no over-award.
risks: The court WILL order us to pay the third-party claimant first. There is no precedent in this corpus where an insurer was completely absolved of paying a third-party death claim due to a licence defect. Every single case orders pay-and-recover.

The claimant will argue that the breach was not 'fundamental' if the driver had ever held a licence (even an expired one). Srinivasamurthy (doc_034) and Iyyapan (doc_032) support a liberal approach to licence defects.

If the owner argues he was unaware the driver had no licence, the court may find no 'conscious breach' and deny recovery. We must lead evidence that the owner knew or ought to have known — e.g., the owner never asked for the licence, or the driver was a known unlicensed person.
The criminal cases (doc_016, doc_017) establish that absence of a licence does not itself prove rash or negligent driving — the claimant still needs to prove negligence caused the accident.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: Claims Tribunal under Section 166 MV Act. Primary relief sought: (a) a finding that the driver had no valid licence constituting a fundamental breach; (b) direction to the owner to pay the compensation; (c) in the alternative, an order that we pay the award and recover the entire sum from the owner in the same proceedings, with liberty to execute through the Tribunal.

caveats: doc_016 (Reserved On vs State of HP) and doc_017 (Sanjay vs State of Haryana) are criminal cases about rash and negligent driving — they do not address insurer civil liability for licence defects and are not relevant to our defence.

doc_009 (Kamal vs Mursleem) concerns contributory negligence of an injured rider who himself had no licence — it is about the claimant's own negligence, not the insurer's defence against a third-party death claim.
doc_005 (L&T Insurance vs Bindudevi) concerns the bar under Section 167 MV Act and workmen's compensation — unrelated to licence-defence issues.
doc_014 (Shivlal vs Rukmabai) concerns gratuitous passengers in goods vehicles — not relevant to our facts.
doc_042 (Nazar Singh vs State of Punjab) concerns employer recovery from an employee-driver after an award — not about insurer liability for licence defects.

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving a motor vehicle without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy, absolving the insurer of direct liability to the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had no driving licence at all on the date of accident — identical to our case. The tribunal held the insurer proved the breach under Section 149(2) and was not directly liable.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the strongest supporting authority in the corpus. It squarely holds that a complete absence of a licence is a 'fundamental breach' and the insurer is not liable to indemnify the insured. The pay-and-recover direction was given only because the claimant was a third party.
supporting.quote: riding/driving vehicle on public road without having driving license it is not only an offense punishable under section 3(1) r/w 181 of MV Act but also fundamental and statutory breach of insurance policy. Hence, the respondent No.2 is not liable to pay the compensation and he is absolved from its liability.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar
